claim: Modeling from memory/imagination alone tends to produce objects that read as subtly wrong, because the brain habitually filters out real-world details it judges unimportant for recognition (illustrated with a doorknob: memory retains 'sphere you grip and turn' but drops the keyhole, privacy lock, and seam details actually present) -- reference images are what surface the details memory silently discards.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~28:50: doorknob example -- memory keeps only the recognizable gist of an object and drops the actual surface detail, illustrated by describing a doorknob from memory versus really looking at one.
rejected_alternative: Modeling a common object (a coffee mug) purely from memory without a reference photo
reason: Objects modeled purely from memory come out looking subtly wrong because memory only retains an abstracted gist, not the actual surface detail a reference photo reveals.

claim: When extruding an appendage (e.g. a mug handle) from a face on a body that already has a Solidify modifier for wall thickness, apply the Solidify modifier to bake it into real geometry BEFORE extruding the appendage -- otherwise the still-live modifier re-applies its thickness effect to the newly extruded handle geometry too, producing a broken double-thickness result on the handle.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~43:39: extruding the handle before applying the Solidify modifier caused the handle geometry itself to pick up an unwanted extra thickness pass from the still-active modifier; applying Solidify first (baking it into real mesh) avoided the problem.
rejected_alternative: Extruding the handle first, then dealing with the modifier
reason: A still-live Solidify modifier applies to whatever mesh exists at evaluation time, including newly-extruded appendage geometry -- baking it into real mesh first means only the intended body picks up the thickness.

claim: Holding Ctrl while right-clicking during appendage extrusion (e.g. building a curved handle segment-by-segment) both extrudes a new segment AND automatically rotates it to align with the surface, replacing the separate Extrude / Grab / Rotate keystrokes normally needed for each segment of a curved, following-the-contour appendage.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~48:38: Ctrl+right-click extrudes and auto-orients the new faces to follow the surface direction, described as most useful specifically for handle-like curved appendages.
rejected_alternative: Separately pressing Extrude, Grab, and Rotate for each segment of a curved handle
reason: The combined shortcut removes several repeated manual steps per segment when building a curved appendage that needs to keep re-orienting to follow a surface.

claim: Extruding a new appendage from a small, low-density patch of a subdivided mesh (e.g. a mug handle base) produces a visibly distorted 'starfish'-like n-gon pattern at the extrusion base unless a loop cut is added close to that patch first, tightening how far the SubD smoothing tapers -- this is the same size/density-evenness cause behind the pinching cluster already documented across multiple other sources, now specifically tied to appendage extrusion.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~41:21: an extrusion point on a low-density mesh area produced a visibly distorted star-shaped artifact under Subdivision Surface; adding a loop cut close to the extrusion point tightened the smoothing and fixed it.

claim: Perfectly straight, uniform edges on a procedurally-generated surface (e.g. a laser-straight icing edge) read as visibly fake, because that kind of flawless regularity doesn't occur in the physical process being represented -- deliberately introducing irregularity into the geometry is what makes it read as physically real rather than obviously computer-generated.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~1:07:11: a perfectly straight edge on a simulated liquid surface was called out as reading as fake specifically because that flawless straightness couldn't occur in the real physical process, and randomizing it fixed the read.
rejected_alternative: Leaving the generated edge perfectly straight/uniform
reason: Real-world irregularity is what signals physical plausibility to a viewer; mathematically perfect regularity is itself the tell that something is artificial.

claim: Proportional Editing (toggle at the top of the 3D viewport) lets a single-vertex transform (G/R/S) affect a falloff radius of nearby geometry instead of just the selected point, with the falloff radius adjustable live during the transform via scroll wheel or Page Up/Page Down -- useful for adding many small, organic-looking irregularities across a surface quickly instead of moving each point individually.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~1:08:19-1:09:xx: proportional editing was used to move many nearby vertices at once with an adjustable falloff, instead of moving each point individually, specifically to add irregular surface variation faster.
rejected_alternative: Moving each vertex individually to add surface variation
reason: Moving points one at a time to add many small irregularities is described as prohibitively slow; a falloff-based tool covers a whole area's worth of variation in one transform.

claim: Deliberately exaggerating an observed real-world detail (more/larger drip variation than a real donut typically has) beyond strict physical accuracy tends to read as more visually appealing than a strictly accurate reproduction -- part of translating reference into art is identifying which observed details are pleasing and amplifying them rather than reproducing the reference exactly.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~1:17:36-1:17:47: after noting real examples of the reference object don't have as much of a particular visual detail, the detail was deliberately exaggerated anyway because it was judged more visually appealing.
rejected_alternative: Matching the reference's actual level of a visual detail exactly
reason: This is a second independent instance (alongside the asymmetric-detail-placement principle already captured from Blender Bros' tertiary-details video) of choosing visual appeal over strict reference accuracy as a deliberate artistic decision.

claim: After baking (applying) all modifiers on a small secondary-detail object, the Sculpt Mode Inflate/Deflate brush is a fast way to add localized swelling/bulge detail at a specific spot (e.g. where a drip pools at its endpoint) that would be tedious to achieve through vertex-level poly editing -- and a separate Grab brush lets you reshape/reposition a region of mesh by dragging, similar to a stronger localized proportional-edit.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~1:27:46-1:28:xx: switched to Sculpt Mode specifically to use the Inflate/Deflate brush for adding localized swelling at drip endpoints, described as more direct than trying to achieve the same result through vertex editing.
rejected_alternative: Trying to add the same localized swelling detail through vertex-level poly editing alone
reason: Poly-editing a small localized bulge with individual vertices was described as finicky; the sculpt brush achieves the same visual result more directly.

claim: A Lattice Deform (select the target mesh(es) plus a new Lattice, deform-selected) gives a non-destructive way to add broad organic deformation to an otherwise-finished mesh -- moving the lattice's own low-resolution control points bends the underlying mesh without touching its actual geometry, and the effect can be applied (baked in) later or discarded entirely by deleting the lattice, useful when a shape needs a broad correction after detail work is already done.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~1:37:00 area: a Lattice Deform was added over an already-detailed mesh specifically to add broad organic variation non-destructively, described as useful precisely because it doesn't require redoing already-completed detail work.
rejected_alternative: Going back into the mesh's own edit mode to add the same broad deformation directly to its vertices
reason: Editing the mesh directly for a broad shape correction after detail work is already in place risks disturbing that detail; a lattice cage isolates the broad deformation from the fine geometry underneath.

claim: Understanding the real-world physical process that produces a form can justify a specific, non-obvious modeling decision that pure visual reference alone might not explain -- e.g. knowing a fried food is cooked half-submerged in oil then flipped explains why its middle band ends up lighter and less puffy than the rest, which then becomes a deliberate, informed shape decision (a slightly concave middle band) rather than a guess.
supporting_evidence: Paraphrased from ~1:31:35 area: a specific asymmetric shape detail (a lighter, less-puffy middle band) was explained and justified by describing the real-world cooking process that produces it, not just copied from a photo without explanation.
rejected_alternative: Modeling the form purely from visual reference without understanding why it looks that way
reason: Knowing the causal process behind a visual detail makes it possible to apply that detail correctly and confidently elsewhere, rather than only being able to copy it where a reference photo happens to show it.
